concept.concept_description:
We conjecture an explicit formula for the Jordan canonical form of the image of a regular unipotent element under any finite‑dimensional irreducible polynomial representation of GL₃(ₖ). Let λ = (a,b,c) be a dominant weight with a > b > c. Define d₁ = a‑ b, d₂ = b‑ c, d₃ = a‑ c and the rational function

M(t) = (1‑ t^{d₁+1})(1‑ t^{d₂+1})(1‑ t^{d₃+2}) /
       ((1‑ t^{d₁})(1‑ t^{d₂})(1‑ t^{d₃})).

Write M(t) = Σ_{j≥0} m_j t^j. Then the Jordan canonical form of π_λ(u) (the regular unipotent u ∈ GL₃(ₖ) under the representation π_λ) is the partition whose parts are (j+1) repeated m_j times. In particular the multiplicities m_j satisfy a linear recurrence with characteristic polynomial (1‑ t^{d₁})(1‑ t^{d₂})(1‑ t^{d₃}).

concept.title: Phantom Topologies: Spaces That Change When You Look at Them
concept.concept_description: What if the topology of a space depended on who is observing it? Define a phantom topology on a set X as a function T: O -> Top(X) that assigns to each observer o a topology T(o) on X. Two observers o1, o2 agree on an open set U if U is open in both T(o1) and T(o2). The phantom number of (X, T) is the minimum number of observers needed to determine the topology: if U is open in every T(o) that contains a point x, then U is a neighborhood of x in the 'real' topology. Conjecture: Every second-countable space (X, tau) admits a phantom representation with at most 2 observers (the real topology is the intersection of two phantom topologies). Moreover, every non-metrizable space requires at least 3 observers. The intuition: the real topology is what ALL observers agree on, and phantom topologies are what individual observers see. Like quantum mechanics, measurement changes the topology. Test: prove that R with the standard topology is the intersection of the lower limit topology and the upper limit topology (2 observers). Prove that the Zariski topology on R^2 requires at least 3 observers. Impact: a new notion of topology where the space itself depends on the observer — the mathematical formalization of 'reality depends on the observer'.

`C(q·p, p) ≡ q (mod p)`.
-/
theorem choose_prime_fibre {q p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) :
    Nat.choose (q * p) p ≡ q [MOD p] := by

  · norm_num [ hp.pos ];

**Fermat fibre.** For every prime `p` and every base `q`, `qᵖ ≡ q (mod p)`.
-/
theorem pow_prime_fibre {q p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) :
    q ^ p ≡ q [MOD p] := by

`C(q·p, p) ≡ qᵖ (mod p)`.
-/

-/

This cycle established that, for every fixed base `q`, every prime `p` satisfies
the congruence `C(qp, p) ≡ qᵖ (mod p)` — both sides collapse to `q` modulo `p`
by Lucas' evaluation of the binomial and Fermat's evaluation of the power. Hence
the congruence `C(qn, n) ≡ qⁿ (mod n)` has infinitely many solutions
unconditionally. We also pinned the base `q` to a single factor of the driver
integer `Aₜ = C(q^{t+1}, qᵗ) − q^{qᵗ}`. The following conjectures push past the
easy prime fibre into the sparse composite regime.

## 1. Infinitely many composite solutions of the shape `n = qᵗ·p`

**Conjecture.** For every prime `q` there are infinitely many pairs `(t, p)` with
`p` a prime distinct from `q`, `p` dividing `Aₜ`, and base-`q` digit sum
`s_q((q−1)p) ≥ (q−1)t`; each such pair gives a composite solution `n = qᵗ·p`.

**The key insight is** that the residuals `Aₜ / q` form a rapidly growing
integer sequence, and a primitive-prime-divisor phenomenon (in the spirit of
Zsygmondy and Carmichael) should force a *new* large prime factor to appear
infinitely often — and a large prime factor automatically clears the linear
digit-sum threshold.

**Why now?** The prime fibre is now completely understood, which cleanly isolates
the composite family as the true frontier, and the exact one-carry valuation of
`Aₜ` removes the base `q` itself from the candidate pool, sharpening the search to
primes `p ≠ q`.

## 2. Arithmetic of the residual `Rₜ = Aₜ / q`

**Conjecture.** Writing `Rₜ = C(q^{t+1}−1, qᵗ−1) − q^{qᵗ−1}`, the residual `Rₜ` is
squarefree for infinitely many `t`, and for every fixed bound `B` all but finitely
many `Rₜ` possess a prime factor exceeding `B`.

**The key insight is** that `Rₜ` is a difference of a Lucas-type binomial and a
pure prime power, so lifting-the-exponent and cyclotomic divisibility control its
factor structure far more tightly than the raw size estimate suggests.

**Why now?** We have just proved that `q ∥ Aₜ` exactly, so the whole
number-theoretic content of `Aₜ` is concentrated in `Rₜ`; understanding `Rₜ` is
the single remaining obstruction to producing composite solutions on demand.

## 3. The digit-sum gate as a near-automatic condition

**Conjecture.** For fixed `q` and fixed `t`, the proportion of primes `p ≤ X` with
`s_q((q−1)p) ≥ (q−1)t` tends to `1` as `X → ∞`; hence the digit-sum gate is
satisfied by asymptotically every admissible prime and only the divisibility
`p | Aₜ` is truly restrictive.

**The key insight is** that base-`q` digit sums of the multiples `(q−1)p`
concentrate around a value proportional to `log p`, so a fixed linear threshold
`(q−1)t` is eventually cleared by all but a vanishing set of primes.

**Why now?** Equidistribution results for digit sums along primes are strong
enough to make this precise, and separating the "easy" digit gate from the "hard"
divisibility gate is exactly what a two-condition existence proof needs.

## 4. A local-to-global law for all composite solutions

**Conjecture.** A composite `n` solves `C(qn, n) ≡ qⁿ (mod n)` if and only if a
local Lucas–Fermat compatibility holds at every prime power exactly dividing `n`;
in particular the sporadic solutions `n = 30` (base 2) and `n = 36` (base 3),
which lie outside the `qᵗ·p` family, are explained by this criterion.

**The key insight is** that the congruence modulo `n` decomposes by the Chinese
Remainder Theorem into independent congruences at each prime-power component,
where Lucas controls the binomial and Kummer controls the carries.

**Why now?** Small-case data already exhibit composite solutions of several
different shapes, signalling that a single unifying local criterion — rather than
one family at a time — is the right organising principle.

## 5. Effective smallest-composite-solution bounds in the base

**Conjecture.** For every prime base `q` there is a composite solution `n` with
`n ≤ q^{C}` for an absolute constant `C`; the minimal composite solutions begin
`m(2) = 12 = 2²·3` and `m(3) = 36 = 2²·3²`.

**The key insight is** that one can hope to *construct* a composite solution for
each base by making a controlled choice of exponent `t` together with a prime
divisor `p` of `Aₜ` whose digit sum is verified in advance, turning an existence
question into an explicit, size-bounded recipe.

**Why now?** With the prime fibre and the valuation of `Aₜ` settled, the only
missing ingredient for an effective bound is a single guaranteed composite
construction, which the data suggest is always small.
